Mutual fund holdings of IT stocks sink to record low in September
articles.text: Mumbai: Indian mutual funds' exposure to Information Technology (IT) stocks fell to an all-time low in September as concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) disruption, weak global client spending and subdued growth prospects weighed on the sector. The decline has pushed frontline IT stocks such as Infosys and TCS, once among fund managers' biggest holdings, out of mutual funds' top holdings lists.IT stocks accounted for 5.3% of mutual funds' equity assets under management (AUM) in September, compared with 7.6% at the end of 2025 and 9.24% at the end of 2024. The sector's weight had touched a record 13.4% at the end of 2021."The correction in Information Technology stocks during 2026 has been a de-rating story more than an earnings story," said Harsh Thakkar, equity research analyst at Samco Securities.135037302The value of mutual funds' IT holdings fell 25% to ₹2.97 lakh crore in September from ₹3.98 lakh crore in December 2025, according to Prime Database. The value had reached a record ₹4.03 lakh crore in November 2025.Infosys, which was among the five largest holdings of mutual funds at the start of 2026, slipped to 10th place in September. TCS has seen a similar decline. The stock, which ranked 10th among mutual fund holdings in 2024 and was among the top 14 in 2025, slipped to 18th place in September.HCL Tech and Tech Mahindra, which ranked 20th and 25th among mutual funds' largest holdings at the beginning of 2026, slipped to 25th and 31st positions, respectively, in September. Wipro fell sharply to 316th place from 88th at the start of 2026 and 56th in 2024.Read more: Mega Jio Platforms IPO to lead Rs 31,663 crore offerings this week; 9 listings lined upMany fund managers have cut their exposure due to uncertainty over the extent of disruption that AI could bring into the software services industry."Revenue growth has remained muted but has not collapsed," said Thakkar. "However, valuations have fallen sharply because investors priced in the potential threat from AI agents to the labour-intensive application development and maintenance business model."Read more: Can Nifty, Sensex rally further or will bears reign in? 5 factors to steer market this weekWeighed down by these concerns, the Nifty IT index till October 8 had shed about 28% in 2026 as against the 14% decline in the Nifty. But, a rebound since then has helped cut losses, with the index running up 11.7% last week, posting its biggest weekly gains in 18 years, amid a sharp sell-off in AI-related semiconductor stocks elsewhere in Asia on concerns over the durability of their recent rally."Promising management commentary, the anti-AI trade turning favourable for Indian IT companies and valuations that are very reasonable at the moment, below their five-year average and closer to the 10-year average," said Kunal Bajaj, research analyst at Choice Institutional Equities.While the industry cut its exposure to IT stocks, fund houses also made some additions to their holdings. In Infosys, funds increased their holdings by 2.7 crore shares to 86 crore shares in September from 83.4 crore shares in December 2025. In TCS, they added 61 lakh shares, taking their holdings to 20.64 crore shares from around 20 crore.Mutual funds also increased their holdings in HCL Tech by 1.8 crore shares to 26.4 crore from 24.6 crore. But, they reduced their holdings in Tech Mahindra by 45 lakh shares to 18.97 crore from 19.42 crore.In Wipro, their holdings fell by 33.96 crore shares to 17.42 crore from 51.39 crore at the beginning of year.

articles.title: Time Lords kill leap seconds, before they become the new Y2K bug
articles.text: The Time Lords at the General Conference on Weights and Measures (GCPM)* have decided to stop introducing leap seconds, citing the likelihood they could cause problems with internet of things devices – and therefore a Y2K scale remediation effort – as a reason for the change. As The Register reported last week, the GCPM works to harmonize Universal Time – UT1, which boffins calculate using the changing speed of Earth’s rotation – and the Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) standard that humans use to set time. We big-brained hominids can set standards but can’t do much about the fact that the speed of Earth’s rotation is variable. When our planet’s spin slows, the GCPM adds leap seconds so that UT1 and UTC are in synch. In recent years, they have even pondered a negative leap second because Earth’s rotation has sped up a little. Like all good standards orgs, the GCPM conducts years-long debates about its work. The topic of leap seconds has very much been on the agenda in recent years, as they’re increasingly hard to implement now that humanity relies on billions of devices that can usefully share the same timing data but may not easily account for leap seconds. The matter came to a head at last week’s 28th meeting of the GCPM, at which Time Lords voted to end use of leap seconds. The possibility of a negative leap second seems to have been a major factor. “A negative leap second has not previously been applied, and it is considered to pose a high risk of causing anomalies and disruption to critical infrastructures that are largely unprepared,” the Time Lords wrote in a resolution posted after their vote. “The preparation would create, for the industries that rely on time synchronization, a need for financial investment, whose amount is estimated to be similar to their preparations for the millennium bug.” Readers may recall that in the late 1990s, the world spent billions of dollars remediating software that, due to sensible-at-the-time memory-saving measures from the early years of business computing, couldn’t comfortably handle dates after December 31, 1999. Historians now cite the global cost of Y2K remediation at $300-$600 billion. It's widely thought that money was not well-spent. The GCPM also worries about connected devices. The growing influence of IoT (Internet of Things) technologies, dispersed multi-sensor systems, smart grids, and virtual services for contemporary society, creates an increasing risk of malfunction in operation of systems and services with the insertion of any leap second, especially with a negative one,” they wrote. Another concern raised in the resolution is: “The use of different mitigation methods for leap second introductions by global service providers in their server systems, in order to avoid time steps, leads to inconsistency in timing between different systems and in the disseminated time and frequency, which do not conform to the SI unit [the standard second].” The world is home to myriad manufacturers of IoT devices, but fewer standards on how they should behave. Some manufacturers therefore build shabbily insecure devices that ship with vulnerable software that allow them to be subverted with malware, or without facilities that allow easy updates. Billions of devices could therefore fail to implement a leap second. That would become a problem because digital certificates include a notbefore value – a time before which the cert won’t be accepted. Many systems that see a misbehaving cert would reject it. It’s therefore conceivable that if a major ISP’s modems could not accommodate a leap second, the extra sliver of time’s introduction could see the carrier’s network decide its own customers are not trustworthy enough to connect. Scenarios like that rather suggest Time Lords have taken a sensibly long view regarding the perhaps-inevitable fallibility of software developers. The GCPM's replacement for leap seconds is to allow UT1 and UTC to diverge by up to 3,600 seconds under a scheme called "Continuous UTC" that comes into force next year. Humanity has lots of practice adding and removing hours thanks to Daylight Saving time, which some want to sunset. ® * The organisation’s formal name is the Conférence générale des poids et mesures, which yields the acronym GCPM
articles.summary: The Time Lords at the General Conference on Weights and Measures (GCPM)* have decided to stop introducing leap seconds, citing the likelihood they could cause problems with internet of things devices

articles.title: Exporters may have to track emissions
articles.text: New Delhi: The government has begun discussions on whether Indian exporters should track indirect emissions across their supply chains as trade partners tighten green requirements and global value chains become increasingly interconnected.The finance and commerce & industry ministries have held preliminary discussions on whether Scope 3 emissions should be measured for exports to all countries, rather than only for markets such as the European Union and the UK, which have introduced Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) measures.Scope 3 emissions cover indirect emissions across a company's value chain, including those linked to purchased goods and services, capital goods, transportation, waste, business travel, employee commuting, leased assets, raw material extraction and the sourcing of imported raw materials. Measuring them is more complex than tracking emissions directly generated by a company or those associated with the energy it purchases.Also Read | Faster services imports threaten to erode cushion against India’s goods trade deficit: Report"There is one thought that measurement of Scope 3 emissions can't be done for the EU alone. It would have to do for all countries because the value chains are linked," said an official, adding that the indirect nature of these emissions makes them particularly challenging to measure, report and mitigate. However, no decision has been taken on the issue.Niti Aayog, in its report titled Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat And Net Zero: Financing Needs, has said that any inclusion of Scope 3 disclosures should be phased and proportionate, beginning with large entities in high-impact sectors to avoid imposing disproportionate compliance burdens on micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and smaller suppliers.135034854The existing CBAM frameworks provide for the determination of direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions covered under Scopes 1 and 2 of the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. Indian exporters of iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen products are already subject to the EU's CBAM.Also Read | What is holding up the US-India trade deal?"The CBAM is already a challenge for us because we don't have basic data on our raw material emissions. Disclosures on Scope 2 are posing a problem, so adding Scope 3 emissions data on what is my electricity provider and transportation would be unviable," said a steel exporter to the EU. Under the EU CBAM, the central platform will open for the sale of CBAM certificates on February 1, 2027. Importers must submit their first annual CBAM declaration and surrender certificates covering all 2026 imports by September 30, 2027.

Banks also count cost of insurance payout curbs
articles.text: Mumbai: Banks are assessing the impact of the proposed insurance commission curbs. Central Bank of India is expecting a 33% drop in bancassurance fees while Canara Bank is estimating a ₹145-crore hit to fee income, according to top executives of these lenders.Axis Bank, meanwhile, is planning to offset the potential loss through higher sales volumes, changes in product mix and alternative fee income, according to its management. HDFC Bank said it is too early to assess the impact.The changes proposed by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) to insurance commissions seek to rein in distribution costs and improve transparency in sales. For banks, which earn commissions by selling policies through their branches and other channels, lower payouts could put pressure on a key source of non-interest income.Central Bank MD and CEO Kalyan Kumar said he expects bancassurance fees to fall to ₹49 crore from ₹76 crore if the proposals take effect in their current form. The business accounts for about 8% of the bank's fee income, according to Kumar."Our Banca insurance fees are ₹76 crore or about 8% of fee income. It will come down to ₹49 crore, which means a 33% income impact as things stand," Kumar said.The bank expects to recover the shortfall once its two new life and general insurance ventures stabilise, and through products such as credit-linked insurance, he said.Canara Bank's management said during an earnings call that it expects a ₹145-crore impact on fee income. Executives at Axis Bank, which reported a 6% YoY increase in fee income to ₹6,381 crore in the September quarter, said the bank is preparing for the changes but has not quantified its exposure."We've done some of the work on our side in terms of what the potential impact could be and how we could mitigate, through a combination of volume, product mix, etc.," Axis Bank's management said during an earnings call.The lender said it expects six to nine months to prepare for the changes and will seek to generate additional fee income from other businesses to cushion the impact.Axis Bank is also betting that lower insurance prices could spur demand, which would allow higher volumes to compensate for reduced commissions, as was seen in higher insurance sales following the reduction in GST on premiums.
articles.summary: Mumbai: Banks are assessing the impact of the proposed insurance commission curbs. Central Bank of India is expecting a 33% drop in bancassurance fees while Canara Bank is estimating a ₹145-crore hit

articles.title: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
articles.text:
Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee-like access” to assess the risks of its models, following through on a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control.

METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems.

A greater role for third-party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large.

articles.title: Can India’s Three-Part Plan Help End the Russia-Ukraine War?
articles.text:
While US President Donald Trump’s efforts focus on building pressure on Russia and Ukraine not to strike each other’s oil refineries, India seems to be involved in broader discussions aimed at achieving a more comprehensive cessation of hostilities, according to a report.
The Geopolitical Monitor report highlights that New Delhi has proposed a three-part truce between Russia and Ukraine that would stop attacks on energy facilities and other infrastructure, ensure the continued flow of grain and energy through Black Sea ports, and end attacks on commercial ships.
The proposal, conveyed to Ukrainian officials during External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s visit to Kyiv in September, goes beyond separate ceasefire initiatives put forward by Turkey, Egypt, and the United States and seeks to address both infrastructure and maritime security while maintaining vital commodity flows, states the report by Nikola Mikovic.
“We have four proposals. The broadest is India’s proposal. We are ready for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, but only in this combination,” the report cited Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha as saying, adding that an energy ceasefire would mean a complete halt to strikes on all energy facilities, including port infrastructure.
The remarks suggest that Kyiv is open to New Delhi’s broader diplomatic initiative. Although the Kremlin also welcomed India’s efforts, Moscow described the plan as “addressing only one specific aspect of a potential settlement”.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also echoed US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s assessment that there were currently “no prospects for a diplomatic resolution to the war”, arguing that the conditions for negotiations were “not yet in place”.
Russia has repeatedly stressed that it is seeking only a “sustainable just peace”, rather than a ceasefire. From Moscow’s perspective, a truce would only give Ukraine time to regroup, rearm, and prepare for another round of fighting. For Kyiv, under the current circumstances, an energy ceasefire alone, without a broader agreement addressing other aspects of the conflict, does not seem particularly useful either, the report stated.
It underscores that although Russia continues to strike Ukrainian power plants daily, Kyiv has also managed to inflict significant damage on Russia’s energy sector. Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have contributed to fuel shortages, with queues at gas stations across the country becoming commonplace and forcing Moscow to suspend fuel exports. Russia, despite its enormous energy resources, is now forced to import fuel not only from neighbouring Kazakhstan and Belarus, but also from India.
Consequently, energy ties between Moscow and New Delhi are no longer one-sided: while Russia continues to supply crude oil to India, it also imports refined petroleum products from its South Asian partner. Even though the world’s most populous country benefits from these trade arrangements, it also has an interest in ending the war through diplomacy and reducing the risks to the global economy, the report pointed out.
India’s economic position also shapes its approach to the conflict. With the IMF raising its GDP growth forecast for the country to 7 per cent, New Delhi has a clear interest in limiting the economic fallout of a prolonged war. Disruptions to energy supplies, maritime trade, and food markets carry costs that extend well beyond Europe, making a ceasefire a matter of economic interest as much as diplomacy, the report added.
–IANS–

articles.title: Rajnath Singh to Represent India at SCO Government Heads Meet in Tajikistan
articles.text:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will visit Tajikistan’s Dushanbe to represent India at the 25th Meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (CHG) of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), which is set to be held on October 19-20.
The meeting will focus on strengthening multilateral cooperation among SCO member states, especially in the areas of trade, economy, investment, connectivity, innovation and cultural-humanitarian exchanges.
The meeting is also expected to review the progress of ongoing cooperation initiatives and consider decisions relating to the Organisation’s financial and institutional functioning, according to the Ministry of Defence statement.
“India remains actively engaged in various SCO mechanisms and continues to contribute to regional cooperation through initiatives in areas such as start-ups and innovation, digital public infrastructure, and people-to-people exchanges. The meeting will provide an opportunity for India to exchange views with other SCO Member States on advancing practical and mutually beneficial cooperation within the Organisation,” the Ministry of Defence mentioned in a statement.
The previous CHG meeting was held in Russia’s Moscow on November 18 last year, where External Affairs Minister (EAM) S. Jaishankar represented India.
The SCO comprises 10 member states — India, Belarus, Iran, Kazakhstan, China, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. It has two observer states – Afghanistan and Mongolia and 15 dialogue partners – Azerbaijan, Armenia, Egypt, Cambodia, Qatar, Kuwait, Laos, Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Sri Lanka.
In September, India highlighted the three pillars of ‘Security, Connectivity, and Opportunity’ for international trade at the 25th meeting of Ministers of the SCO Member States Responsible for Foreign Economic and Trade Activities held in Tajikistan’s Dushanbe, according to an official statement.
The meeting reviewed ongoing cooperation among SCO member states in the areas of economic and trade activities and exchanged views on measures to further deepen trade and economic cooperation within the SCO framework.
In his intervention on behalf of India, Additional Secretary, Commerce, Yashvir Singh underscored the significant economic potential of the SCO and the importance of translating this potential into tangible outcomes through increased intra-SCO trade, lower trade costs, resilient supply chains, and enhanced connectivity.
Referring to the vision articulated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO Summit in Bishkek, India highlighted the three pillars of Security, Connectivity and Opportunity, underscoring their economic significance, particularly in strengthening supply-chain resilience, developing efficient and trusted connectivity, and expanding opportunities for businesses through greater market access.
India also emphasised the important role of trade facilitation and digitalisation in reducing the cost and time associated with trade. In this context, it stressed the need for simplified customs procedures, paperless trade and electronic exchange of documents, alongside stronger multimodal connectivity and reduced transit times.
It also called for greater cooperation among SCO Member States to diversify and strengthen supply chains in strategic and emerging sectors, including agriculture, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing, and electronics. The potential for enhanced cooperation in energy security, renewable energy, and green hydrogen was also emphasised.
Source: IANS

articles.title: Defence Ministry Reviews SMPP After Bribery Allegations
articles.text:
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) may have put the screws on India’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) over allegations of a bribery scandal in a ₹500-crore ammunition deal with state-run Munitions India Limited (MIL).The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) may have put the screws on India’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) over allegations of a bribery scandal in a ₹500-crore ammunition deal with state-run Munitions India Limited (MIL). This shift could impact the company’s chances of winning new defence contracts if it is formally suspended.
SMPP’s defence firm is now on trial after the CBI arrested Ashish Kansal, CEO-Director-Promoter of the company and Anil Kumar, Executive Director of MIL, Kumar’s brother, B Harshavardhan in October. The agency registered the case on 12 October, and arrested the people on 13 October. It is investigating allegations of illegal gratification in exchange for official favours and the disclosure of sensitive information relating to defence production and procurement.
The threat against SMPP comes as revised government guidelines on penalties for business dealings with entities. The provisions empower the competent authority to put on hold business activities during the course of investigation of allegations, including when information received from investigators about the initiation of a criminal investigation, or an FIR filed by an investigative agency.
As per the document excerpt provided for this report, the Secretary of the department concerned may suspend pending a full proceeding or on receiving information in regard to a criminal investigation or FIR. It also includes a review process after six months and extensions should be done in accordance with the prescribed procedure. The length of time and extent of action against SMPP will vary according to the order made by the competent authority.
A suspension would have significant commercial consequences. In accordance with the applicable procurement process, the entity whose business activity is suspended loses the opportunity to become a party to future bids subject to the order, and the issuing of new requests for offers is not allowed to it. It may also apply to allied firms but the extent of the order would depend on the provisions and government’s discretion.
Beyond the early pulp packaging days, SMPP has grown into the Defence sector, with a range of equipment including ballistic protection products, products for ammunition and drone systems. The suspension could impact the firm’s ability to secure new defence deals as a result of its government procurement business. The impact on any exceptions and existing contracts, however, would be determined by the final terms of the order and relevant procurement guidelines.

articles.title: DRDO Moves to Develop Airborne Laser Power System
articles.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has floated a tender for one airborne liquid-cooled power converter system for a laser system, illustrating yet another sign of interest in the power and thermal-management needs of an airborne laser weapon.
The GeM bid, GEM/2026/B/8103106, was published on September 30 and closes on November 4, 2026. The tender is being issued from Hyderabad under the Department of Defence Research & Development and the value is not publicly disclosed. The item is described as an “Airborne Liquid Cooled Power Converter System For Laser System” with a quantity of one.
That combination is noteworthy because an airborne laser requires significantly more than the laser source alone. The power converter would condition and convert the platform’s electrical power to the form needed by the laser and associated electronics. Liquid cooling, on the other hand, could assist in balancing the heat generated by high-power electronics within the limited weight and volume constraints of an airborne platform.
Another DRDO tender issued from Hyderabad on the same day seeks one airborne battery system for a high-power laser system, under GeM bid GEM/2026/B/8096622. BidEasy DRDO has also floated a separate requirement including the development of a latent-heat-storage-based thermal-management system for airborne applications, including a prototype unit.
Together, the requirements illustrate the support infrastructure needed to operate high-power equipment in an airborne environment. However, there is no public confirmation that all three tenders make up a single weapon programme. DRDO has showcased the GoAL – Airborne Laser DEW Pod concept, illustrated on a helicopter, including an MWIR sensor, laser range finder and beam director.

articles.title: Why the Indian Air Force Relies on a Two-Crew Su-30MKI
articles.text:
The decision to field the Su-30MKI as a two-crew aircraft pilot up front, Weapon Systems Officer in the rear wasn’t an accident of design lineage. It reflects a deliberate operational philosophy built around what a heavy, long-range multirole fighter is actually asked to do.
Kindly note, the Su-30MKI isn’t a pure air-superiority interceptor it’s designed to simultaneously handle air dominance, deep interdiction, and precision strike across genuinely long ranges. Managing that scope of mission — radar tracking, sensor fusion across radar/infrared/electronic warfare inputs, weapons targeting, navigation, and threat prioritisation while also physically flying a supermaneuverable, thrust-vectoring aircraft is simply too much for one person to do well under combat stress. Splitting that load lets the pilot stay focused on flying and tactical positioning while the WSO manages sensors, targeting, and the broader tactical picture from the rear cockpit.
This is where the twin-seat configuration earns its keep on paper versus in theory. On extended missions —and the Su-30MKI, with aerial refuelling, is built for genuinely long-range strike and standoff missions a single pilot juggling flight control and complex mission systems for hours degrades in performance well before a shared-workload crew does. Two crew members trading focus keeps both flying and weapons management sharp deep into a sortie, rather than one person’s attention fraying on both fronts simultaneously.
There’s also a safety dimension that’s easy to overlook. If the pilot becomes incapacitated, overwhelmed, or disoriented in a high-stress combat scenario, the rear-seat WSO who typically has flight-qualification themselves can take over navigation, communication, or emergency procedures. That’s not a trivial margin in a $60-70 million-plus aircraft operating deep in contested or high-threat airspace.
Kindly note, India’s approach here mirrors an established global pattern for heavy multirole fighters rather than inventing something new. The American F-15E Strike Eagle, the F/A-18F Super Hornet, and Russia’s own Su-34 all follow the same two-crew philosophy for comparable reasons — deep interdiction missions specifically benefit from a dedicated second crew member handling ground-mapping radar and targeting pods while the pilot concentrates purely on threat avoidance and flight path. The Su-30MKI sits squarely in that same category of aircraft, just built around Russian airframe heritage rather than American.
This operational lesson has stuck with the IAF well beyond the Su-30MKI itself. During the original Indo-Russian FGFA programme, India specifically pushed for a two-seat configuration, explicitly wanting to replicate the Su-30MKI’s proven crew model on a fifth-generation platform. That preference has resurfaced recently with Russia reportedly offering India a twin-seat Su-57 variant, where the rear-seat WSO would function less as a traditional weapons operator and more as a mission commander overseeing manned-unmanned teaming with accompanying drones essentially evolving the same core division-of-labour philosophy that made the Su-30MKI’s two-crew setup work, adapted for a battlefield where one crew member may soon be commanding unmanned wingmen rather than just managing sensors.

articles.title: Issuance of Rs 56.8 crore tender by Bharat Dynamics Ltd to its former CMD’s company under scanner
articles.text:
New Delhi: A Rs 56.8 crore tender issued by Bharat Dynamics Ltd (BDL) in May for the supply of optical sights to a company run by its former chairman and managing director has brought the defence public sector undertaking under scrutiny over potential conflict-of-interest concerns.
The controversy follows a report by The Indian Express that the Hyderabad-based defence PSU, citing “urgency”, issued a single tender for the optical sights to Aindri Defence Advisory Private Limited, a company set up by former BDL CMD Commodore Siddharth Mishra (Retd) and his wife after his retirement. His wife holds 95 percent stake in the company.
Mishra headed BDL from March 2019 to March 2023. He is currently serving as a member of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
The tender covers the supply of 300 optical sights, with delivery required within seven months of the completion of acceptance and validation tests of five sample units supplied by the company.
Sources in the defence establishment told ThePrint that Aindri has supplied five sample units, all of which have cleared technical inspection by BDL. The financial evaluation of the company’s bid is underway, and no contract has been signed yet, they added.
Sources said due process had been followed in issuing the tender but declined to elaborate on the urgency cited to justify the single-tender route.
The delay in finalising the contract has also raised questions about the urgency cited for the procurement, given that the tender was issued in May and the financial evaluation remains underway.
An open tender allows multiple vendors to compete, potentially helping the procuring organisation secure more competitive prices. In urgent cases, however, procurement rules permit a restricted or single-tender process, subject to the applicable rules and approval requirements.
The circumstances surrounding the procurement, including the justification for urgency and the decision to invite only one company, are therefore key.
Sources explained that there is no general prohibition on former public-sector executives setting up businesses in the same sector after retirement. However, the fact that the company is linked to a former head of the procuring PSU raises questions about safeguards against actual or perceived conflicts of interest.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)
